title: A sharp gradient-corrected Lieb--Thirring inequality in one dimension with applications to density functional theory
abstract: We first prove a sharp Lieb-Thirring inequality with semi-classical constant and gradient correction in one dimension. In the periodic setting, the corresponding inequality also includes a parity dependent shell-correction term, which appears to be new. Moreover, we also characterize the optimizers of these inequalities. In particular, the optimizing density profiles form a two-dimensional manifold, which we call here the Poincaré density manifold.   We then apply these results to study the Thomas--Fermi--von Weizsäcker (TFW) approximation of the kinetic energy in Density Functional Theory. More precisely, we first obtain an explicit and non-asymptotic bound on the global and local error made by the TFW approximation. These bounds are controlled by the distance of the normalized density profile from the Poincaré density manifold times the number of particles. In particular, these bounds show that the TFW approximation is exact on the Poincaré manifold. We then show that, in the periodic setting, the distance between the Kohn-Sham potential and the inverse TFW potential in the natural dual Sobolev space can also be controlled by explicit density dependent constants times the distance to the Poincaré manifold. As a corollary, we prove that for a fixed density profile, the Kohn-Sham potential converges towards the inverse Thomas--Fermi potential in the high-density limit $N \rightarrow \infty$ with asymptotic rate of order $N^{-2}$. This rate is shown to be optimal.
summary: This paper develops sharp, gradient-corrected Lieb-Thirring inequalities in one dimension and applies them to rigorously analyze the Thomas-Fermi-von Weizsäcker (TFW) approximation in DFT. The main achievement is establishing precise error bounds that show the TFW approximation is exact on specific optimal density manifolds, confirming the convergence rate of the Kohn-Sham potential in the high-density limit.
main_problem: To derive sharp, gradient-corrected Lieb-Thirring inequalities in one dimension and apply these results to rigorously analyze the Thomas-Fermi-von Weizsäcker (TFW) approximation in Density Functional Theory (DFT).
main_result: The paper establishes sharp inequalities and derives non-asymptotic error bounds showing that the TFW approximation is exact on the Poincaré density manifold, leading to an optimal $N^{-2}$ convergence rate for the Kohn-Sham potential in the high-density limit.
method: The work uses advanced mathematical techniques involving functional analysis, spectral theory (Lieb-Thirring inequalities), and rigorous error estimation based on Poincaré deficits.
model_or_system: The study concerns the electronic structure of quantum systems modeled by DFT in one dimension, using density profiles ($ho$) and single-particle density matrices ($\gamma$). The analysis compares the exact kinetic energy functional with the TFW approximation.
key_observables: Kinetic energy functional ($T[\gamma]$), gradient correction term ($G(ho)$), Poincaré deficit ($\delta_P(ho)$), and the difference between the Kohn-Sham and TFW potentials.
important_parameters: Number of particles ($N$), dimensionality (one dimension, $\mathbb{R}$ or Torus $\mathbb{T}$), and the distance of the density profile from the Poincaré manifold.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on establishing sharp inequalities and assuming the existence of specific optimizing density profiles that define the Poincaré manifold.
figures_summary: Not specified in the provided notes, but Figure 1 is mentioned to show density profiles and Kohn-Sham potentials for $N=3$ in the torus case.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first proving sharp, gradient-corrected Lieb-Thirring inequalities in 1D (on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{T}$). It then applies these results to derive rigorous, non-asymptotic error bounds for the TFW approximation, culminating in the proof of the optimal $N^{-2}$ convergence rate for the Kohn-Sham potential.
why_interesting: This work provides highly rigorous mathematical justifications for approximations used in DFT, which is a cornerstone theory for understanding electronic structure in materials and molecules, connecting fundamental inequalities to practical computational methods.
